findings.claim: In November 2022 Walmart agreed to pay $3.1 billion to settle opioid lawsuits by state and local governments over prescriptions filled at its pharmacies, without admitting liability. Nebraska’s attorney general noted it had filled significantly fewer opioid prescriptions than CVS or Walgreens.

In August 2026 Walmart settled the Justice Department’s 2020 civil suit alleging its pharmacies unlawfully filled opioid prescriptions from 2013, without admitting liability. Reports put the payment at $50 million, which Walmart called immaterial; it also signed a DEA agreement on monitoring future dispensing.

A whistleblower False Claims Act case filed in 2019, alleging Walmart breached the Controlled Substances Act and state pharmacy rules, was settled in 2026 for an amount Walmart called immaterial, without admitting liability. The Justice Department had declined to intervene.

In February 2026 Walmart agreed, without admitting liability, to a $100 million judgment, about $63 million of it suspended, to settle FTC and 11-state charges that it misled Spark delivery drivers about pay and tips and told customers all tips went to drivers. The order requires an earnings-verification program, with practices and reporting kept for ten years.

In June 2025 Walmart agreed to a $10 million judgment to settle an FTC suit filed in 2022 alleging that, from 2013 to 2018, it let scammers use its money transfer services by failing to adopt effective anti-fraud measures, train staff or warn customers.

In December 2024 the CFPB sued Walmart and Branch Messenger, alleging unfair, deceptive and abusive practices over deposit accounts opened for delivery drivers. The Bureau dismissed the case with prejudice in May 2025; no court ruled on the allegations.

In June 2019 Walmart paid about $282.7 million to resolve DOJ and SEC Foreign Corrupt Practices Act investigations into internal controls at subsidiaries in Brazil, Mexico, India and China before 2011, under a non-prosecution agreement; its Brazilian subsidiary pleaded guilty to a books-and-records charge.

In its filing for the quarter to July 2026, Walmart reported pending matters: opioid cases in the federal MDL and in Canada, equal-pay claims by about 77,000 current and former Asda store staff that it partly indemnifies, its appeal of a Mexican antitrust fine, and Indian competition and investment proceedings against Flipkart.
Walmart disclosed $7.84 million in US federal lobbying expenses for 2025. Its employee-funded PAC gave 55.2% of its federal contributions to Republicans and 44.8% to Democrats that year.

In December 2024 Walmart said it would likely miss its targets to cut emissions from its own operations by 35% by 2025 and 65% by 2030 from 2015 levels. Those emissions rose 3.9% in 2023, which Walmart put down partly to ageing refrigeration and transport, and were 19.3% below 2015.

Rob Walton gave $17.6 million in the 2024 election cycle, mainly to Republicans, per OpenSecrets data reported by the Deseret News, which also reported his $1 million gift to a super PAC backing Senator John Curtis. OpenSecrets reported he gave $5 million to the Koch network’s AFP Action super PAC in April 2023.

Rob Walton was a named defendant in a Delaware shareholder derivative suit alleging Walmart directors and officers failed to oversee opioid dispensing. It settled for $123 million paid by insurers to Walmart, plus governance commitments, approved in December 2024; defendants denied wrongdoing.
The Rob and Melani Walton Foundation, with Rob Walton as director and president, reported charitable disbursements of about $108.5 million in 2024 and $79.7 million in 2023 in its IRS filings.

ecology.reason: Mass retail and logistics. In December 2024 Walmart said it would likely miss its 2025 and 2030 targets for emissions from its own operations, which rose in 2023 with transport and ageing refrigeration and stood 19.3% below 2015.

politics.reason: Major donor: Rob Walton gave $17.6 million in the 2024 election cycle, mainly to Republicans (OpenSecrets data), and $5 million to the Koch network’s AFP Action in 2023. Walmart itself reported $7.84 million in federal lobbying in 2025, which is ordinary corporate lobbying.

social.reason: Walmart agreed in 2022 to a $3.1 billion settlement of opioid lawsuits over prescriptions filled at its pharmacies, without admitting liability; officials noted it filled fewer opioid prescriptions than CVS or Walgreens. It settled the federal opioid suit in 2026 and FTC charges over delivery-driver pay the same year, without admitting liability.

legal.reason: Company settlement above $1 billion (opioids, 2022), plus smaller settlements and a 2019 guilty plea by a Brazilian subsidiary over bribery controls. Rob Walton was a named defendant in a shareholder suit over opioid oversight, settled in 2024 for $123 million paid by insurers, with no admission and no personal penalty.

unresolved.reason: Pending company-level matters: opioid cases in the US and Canada, equal-pay claims by about 77,000 Asda store staff that Walmart partly indemnifies, and antitrust proceedings in Mexico and India. The federal opioid suit was settled in 2026. The opioid shareholder suit naming Rob Walton was settled in 2024; no pending personal matter found.

proposal.counterweights: The Rob and Melani Walton Foundation, which he leads, disbursed about $108.5 million in 2024 and $79.7 million in 2023 (IRS filings).
proposal.rationale: Politics 1 to 2: $17.6m in one cycle and $5m to one super PAC is major-donor scale, below the very largest US donors, so not 3. Unresolved 0 to 2: Walmart reports several pending company cases (f8); the personal derivative suit is settled. Legal stays 2: the personal settlement was paid by insurers with no penalty (R3).

results.comment: Supported by the AP report (15 Nov 2022: $3.1bn proposed, no admission of liability, Nebraska AG's comparison with CVS and Walgreens) and the 2026 Reuters report (Walmart agreed to pay $3.1bn in 2022).

Supported: Reuters (28 Aug 2026) gives the December 2020 DOJ suit, conduct from 2013, no admission and Walmart's 'immaterial' wording; Gray News gives $50 million and the DEA memorandum of agreement; the 10-Q confirms settlement without admitting liability.
Supported by the 10-Q: qui tam filed 23 Aug 2019, DOJ declined to intervene, relators allege CSA and state pharmacy rule breaches, settled without admitting liability for an immaterial amount.

Rewritten: the 10-year term in the 10-Q covers 'programmatic practices and reporting obligations', not earnings verification as such; the claim now says so, and adds 'without admitting liability' from the 10-Q. Amounts, 11 states and charges match the FTC release (26 Feb 2026) and the 10-Q.
Supported by the FTC release (20 Jun 2025): $10m stipulated judgment, complaint filed 2022, conduct 2013-2018, failures on anti-fraud policies, training and warnings.
Supported by the CFPB page: filed 23 Dec 2024, unfair, deceptive and abusive practices alleged, voluntarily dismissed with prejudice on 13 May 2025, no merits ruling.

Supported: Walmart's 8-K release gives $282.7m, the DOJ non-prosecution agreement, the guilty plea by WMT Brasilia to causing a books-and-records violation, the four countries and controls before April 2011; CBS/AP confirms the amount and date.

Supported by the 10-Q for the quarter ended 31 July 2026: opioid MDL cases and two Canadian class actions pending, about 77,000 Asda equal-value claimants with partial indemnity, Walmex appeal of the COFECE fine, and Indian ED and CCI proceedings against Flipkart. All company-level.
Supported by Walmart's public policy page: $7.84m federal lobbying in 2025, employee-funded WALPAC split 55.2% Republican and 44.8% Democratic.

Supported: Trellis gives the 18 Dec 2024 disclosure, the 3.9% rise in 2023 and 19.3% below 2015; Reuters (via ThePrint) gives the 35%/65% targets against 2015 and the refrigeration and transport drivers.

The $17.6m (2024 cycle, mainly Republicans, OpenSecrets) and the $5m to AFP Action in April 2023 (OpenSecrets via Raw Story, which names Rob and Jim) are supported.
